chapters.title: So Soon Removed
chapters.teaser: Paul opens with shock, not greeting — astonished the Galatians abandoned the gospel this fast.
body: Paul skips something every other one of his letters includes: an opening word of thanks for the church he's writing to. Galatians goes straight from a brief greeting to shock — "I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel" (v.6). The missing thanksgiving is itself part of the message: Paul is too alarmed to open with pleasantries.

He adds immediately that what they're being offered "is not another" gospel (v.7) — not a variant worth debating, but something wearing the gospel's name while being nothing like it. That distinction sets the urgency for everything the letter will go on to argue.

chapters.title: Let Him Be Accursed
chapters.teaser: Paul pronounces the same curse twice, even against an angel who might preach a different gospel.
body: Paul pronounces the same curse twice in a row: "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed" (v.8), repeated almost word for word in verse 9. The doubling signals this isn't a line tossed off in anger — Paul wants it stated as deliberately as possible.

Naming "an angel from heaven" in the warning matters. The danger he's describing isn't a message that will look obviously wrong — it's one that could arrive wrapped in real spiritual authority and still be corrosive. Source and credentials, in Paul's view, don't excuse corrupted content.

chapters.title: Not Trying to Please Men
chapters.teaser: Paul frames his entire ministry as a test of whether he serves God's approval or people's.
body: Paul answers critics who were apparently accusing him of softening the law to win Gentile converts: "do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (v.10). He treats the accusation as worth refuting at the very start of the letter.

The verse sets up a contrast that runs through the whole letter — gospel truth and social comfort pulling in opposite directions. Paul treats his own willingness to offend people as proof of his integrity, not something to be embarrassed about.

chapters.title: A Gospel Received by Revelation
chapters.teaser: Paul insists his gospel came directly from Christ, not secondhand from the Jerusalem apostles.
body: Paul makes a bold claim about where his gospel came from: "I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ" (v.12). He isn't presenting himself as a student relaying someone else's teaching — he's claiming to be a direct recipient of the message itself.

That claim sets up the argument to come. If rivals in Galatia were saying Paul's gospel was just a watered-down version of what the "real" apostles taught, he's establishing here that his gospel has its own independent, divine origin — not a derivative one that others could correct.

chapters.title: From Persecutor to Preacher
chapters.teaser: Paul recounts going to Arabia, not Jerusalem, deliberately avoiding dependence on the other apostles.
body: Paul describes his own calling as entirely God's doing, not something he worked his way into. After persecuting the church "beyond measure" (v.13), he says God "separated me from my mother's womb... to reveal his Son in me" — and his very next move was to go to Arabia, not Jerusalem (v.15-16).

The geography itself is the argument. Three years passed before Paul even met Peter, and only briefly (v.18); the Judean churches knew him only by reputation (v.22-23). He's building a timeline with no room in it for the idea that his gospel was borrowed or supervised by anyone else.

chapters.title: Titus Not Compelled
chapters.teaser: A Greek companion becomes a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.
body: Fourteen years later, Paul brings an uncircumcised Greek named Titus to Jerusalem, and reports the result plainly: "neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised" (v.3). One man's specific case becomes the proof of a principle Paul will spend the rest of the letter defending.

He names the opposing pressure directly — "false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage" (v.4). Titus's uncircumcised status wasn't incidental; it was contested, and holding the line on it mattered to Paul as nothing less than "the truth of the gospel" (v.5).

chapters.title: The Right Hand of Fellowship
chapters.teaser: Jerusalem's leading apostles formally recognize Paul's Gentile mission as equal, not subordinate.
body: Jerusalem's leading apostles — "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars" — formally recognized Paul's mission by giving him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship" (v.9). This wasn't Paul asking Jerusalem's permission; it was two parallel missions, Peter's to the circumcised and Paul's to the Gentiles, acknowledging each other as equals.

Paul adds a pointed detail: "they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me" (v.6). He isn't dismissing Jerusalem's authority — he's insisting his gospel needed no correction or addition from them. The relationship he's describing is equality, not subordination.

chapters.title: Withstanding Peter to His Face
chapters.teaser: Paul publicly confronts the leading apostle over a lapse into exclusionary table practice.
body: Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers in Antioch — until certain people arrived from James, and "he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision" (v.12). Even Barnabas got swept into the same reversal (v.13). Paul doesn't handle this quietly: "I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed" (v.11).

The confrontation shows the stakes were practical, not just doctrinal. Withdrawing from a shared meal communicated that Gentile believers were second-class, no matter what anyone officially taught. For Paul, behavior could deny the gospel just as surely as bad doctrine could.

chapters.title: Justified by Faith, Not Works
chapters.teaser: Paul states the letter's central thesis in a single dense sentence to Peter's face.
body: Paul states the letter's central thesis right to Peter's face, repeating it three times in a single verse for emphasis: "a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ... for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified" (v.16). Everything else in Galatians will argue, illustrate, and defend this one claim.

"Works of the law" likely points especially at boundary markers like circumcision and food laws — the very practices that had just divided the Antioch table. Paul isn't dismissing the law's value altogether; he's denying that it's the basis on which anyone is declared right with God.

chapters.title: Crucified With Christ
chapters.teaser: Paul describes his own identity as having died and been replaced by Christ living in him.
body: Paul describes his own identity in some of the most personal language in any of his letters: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me" (v.20). This isn't a general doctrine of salvation — it's Paul describing his own remade self.

He closes the chapter with the sharpest stakes he can state: "I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain" (v.21). Going back to law-based righteousness wouldn't just be a weaker path — it would make Christ's death pointless.

chapters.title: Foolish Galatians, Bewitched
chapters.teaser: Paul opens the chapter's argument with blunt astonishment rather than gentle correction.
body: Paul opens this chapter's argument with blunt astonishment, not gentle correction: "O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?" (v.1). The language of sorcery is deliberate — he's suggesting they've been manipulated into forgetting something they once saw with total clarity.

"Evidently set forth, crucified" recalls how vividly Paul had first preached Christ to them. The tragedy, as he frames it, isn't ignorance — it's amnesia. They knew this once, and something has clouded it since.

chapters.title: Received by Hearing, Not Working
chapters.teaser: Paul appeals to the Galatians' own experience: the Spirit came before any law-keeping began.
body: Paul asks a question he expects to answer itself: "received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?" (v.2). The Galatians became believers and visibly received the Spirit entirely apart from circumcision or keeping the Torah — their own history already disproves the argument being pressed on them now.

He names the exact danger in the next line: "having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?" (v.3). It isn't that they're rejecting Christ outright — it's that they're adding law-keeping on top of him, as if grace alone were an unfinished start needing human effort to complete it.

chapters.title: Abraham Believed God
chapters.teaser: Paul roots his gospel in Genesis, arguing Abraham himself was justified by faith, not law.
body: Paul roots his gospel in Genesis itself: "even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness" (v.6, quoting Genesis 15:6). Abraham was declared righteous centuries before the law existed at Sinai — so if righteousness by faith predates the law, the law can't be its real basis.

He then extends Abraham's status to anyone sharing his faith, regardless of ethnicity: "they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham" (v.9). The rival teachers had appealed to Abraham as father of the circumcised; Paul turns that same appeal into an argument for including the Gentiles.

chapters.title: Redeemed From the Curse
chapters.teaser: Paul explains Christ's crucifixion as absorbing a curse the law itself pronounced.
body: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 to set an impossibly high bar: "cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them" (v.10). Anyone trying to earn righteousness through law-keeping, he argues, is actually standing under that curse's threat, not free from it.

He then applies Deuteronomy 21:23's language about executed criminals directly to the crucifixion: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (v.13). Christ absorbs the very curse the law pronounces on everyone who fails to keep it.

chapters.title: The Law as Schoolmaster
chapters.teaser: Paul compares the law to a guardian who supervises children only until they come of age.
body: Paul compares the law to a household role familiar to his readers: "the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster" (v.24-25). The Greek word paidagogos named a slave who escorted children to school and enforced discipline — a temporary, custodial job, not the source of a child's eventual freedom.

The chapter closes with one of the boldest social claims in the New Testament: "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (v.28). Identity markers that had structured the entire ancient world dissolve into a single new status — belonging to Christ.

chapters.title: The Fulness of Time
chapters.teaser: Paul describes God's rescue as arriving at a specific, chosen moment in history through a human birth.
body: Paul describes God's rescue as arriving at a specific, chosen moment rather than an emergency improvisation: "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" (v.4-5). The incarnation, in his framing, was a planned arrival.

"Made under the law" matters for the letter's whole argument. Christ didn't sidestep the law's demands — he fully entered under them, fulfilling what they required, so that people under the law could be redeemed rather than simply excused.

chapters.title: Abba, Father
chapters.teaser: Paul describes the Spirit crying an intimate Aramaic word for "Father" from inside believers' hearts.
body: Paul describes an intimate shift happening inside believers: "because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father" (v.6). Abba is close, familial language — nearer to "Dad" than a formal title — describing more than a legal change of status.

He completes the logic in the next line: "wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ" (v.7). Adoption isn't a technicality — it comes with the full relational and material standing of a child, not a servant working for status.

chapters.title: Turning Back to Weak Elements
chapters.teaser: Paul is baffled that Gentile converts would willingly return to religious observances resembling their old paganism.
body: Paul is baffled that his Gentile converts would willingly return to something resembling the paganism they'd left behind: "how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage? Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years" (v.9-10). Their new fascination with law-keeping struck him as a regression disguised as spiritual progress.

His next line reveals real pastoral fear, not just doctrinal disagreement: "I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain" (v.11). Paul isn't debating an abstract point here — he's watching people he loves head toward what he sees as a step backward.

chapters.title: Travailing in Birth Again
chapters.teaser: Paul describes his anguish over the Galatians using the image of a mother in ongoing labor.
body: Paul reaches for an unusually maternal image to describe his anguish over the Galatians: "my little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (v.19). He isn't a father giving instructions here — he's a mother enduring repeated labor pains, because their formation in Christ still isn't finished.

He admits he doesn't fully know how to reach them from a distance: "I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you" (v.20). The tenderness in this line sits right alongside the sharper rhetoric around it — anger and anguish, side by side.

chapters.title: Hagar and Sarah as Allegory
chapters.teaser: Paul reads Abraham's two sons as symbols of two covenants — one enslaving, one free.
body: Paul reads Abraham's two sons as symbols of two covenants: "Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman... which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants" (v.22-24). Hagar and Sinai represent slavery; Sarah and "Jerusalem which is above" represent freedom — and choosing law-based righteousness, in this reading, means choosing the slave-born line over the promised one.

He applies Genesis 21's family conflict directly to the Galatian crisis: "cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman" (v.30). Paul treats the choice in front of his readers as no less consequential than Sarah's original demand.

chapters.title: Stand Fast in Liberty
chapters.teaser: Paul opens the chapter with a direct command: don't return to a yoke Christ already removed.
body: Paul turns the whole letter's argument into a direct command: "stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage" (v.1). Everything argued theologically in chapters 1-4 lands here as an imperative addressed to the Galatians' present choice.

He states the stakes as starkly as he can: "if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing" (v.2). This isn't a minor practice Paul is indifferent to — adding law-keeping as a requirement for righteousness cancels, in his view, the very thing that made Christ's death meaningful.

chapters.title: A Little Leaven
chapters.teaser: Paul warns that a small compromise, left unchecked, will eventually corrupt the whole community.
body: Paul reuses a proverb he also applies in 1 Corinthians 5:6, this time to doctrine instead of behavior: "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (v.9). The image assumes leaven never stays contained — even a small addition of law-based requirement will eventually spread through the whole gospel message.
That's why Paul treats what might look like a minor ritual dispute — circumcision — with such urgency throughout the letter. In his experience, small theological compromises rarely stay small.

chapters.title: Liberty as Servanthood
chapters.teaser: Paul defines Christian freedom not as autonomy but as freedom to serve others through love.
body: Paul heads off a misreading of freedom before it can take hold: "ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another" (v.13). Freed from law as a means of earning righteousness, believers aren't released from all obligation — they're freed for a different kind, chosen rather than imposed.

He answers anyone worried that dropping law-keeping means dropping moral seriousness: "all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (v.14). Love doesn't relax what the law actually intended — it fulfills it.

chapters.title: Flesh Against Spirit
chapters.teaser: Paul describes an internal conflict that keeps believers from simply doing whatever they want.
body: Paul describes a real, ongoing internal tension: "the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would" (v.17). Freedom from the law doesn't mean freedom from struggle — it relocates the struggle from external rule-keeping to internal allegiance.

His alternative to both legalism and license is simply this: "if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law" (v.18). Not rules, and not unrestrained impulse — just an ongoing, responsive relationship rather than either a rulebook or a blank check.

chapters.title: Flesh's Works vs Spirit's Fruit
chapters.teaser: Paul contrasts two catalogues of behavior — one a list of works, the other a single fruit.
body: Paul lists the "works of the flesh" (v.19-21) — adultery, hatred, strife, envyings — as a scattered plural catalogue, a pile of separate acts. Against it he sets "the fruit of the Spirit" (v.22-23) as a single, grammatically singular thing: love, joy, peace, and the rest read as one integrated whole, not a checklist to pick items from.

The grammar carries the theology. Flesh produces isolated, disconnected acts; the Spirit produces one coherent character. "Against such there is no law" (v.23) — a life shaped this way doesn't need external rules, because it already lines up with what the law was pointing toward all along.

chapters.title: Bearing One Another's Burdens
chapters.teaser: Paul asks the spiritually strong to restore, not condemn, those caught in failure.
body: Paul sets restoration, not judgment, as the community's default response to failure: "brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" (v.1). The warning against self-righteousness is built right into the instruction.

He then deliberately echoes 5:14's summary of the law as love: "bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (v.2). Carrying each other's weight, in Paul's picture, is simply what love looks like in everyday, practical terms.

chapters.title: Sowing to the Spirit
chapters.teaser: Paul closes the letter's ethical section with the same agricultural logic he used for giving elsewhere.
body: Paul applies a simple, unavoidable principle to spiritual life: "be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" (v.7-8). Outcomes follow investment, not intention alone.

He then names the gap where discouragement tends to creep in: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not" (v.9). Sowing and reaping are never simultaneous, and the delay between them is exactly where people give up.

chapters.title: See How Large a Letter
chapters.teaser: Paul draws attention to his own handwriting, underlining the letter's urgency with a physical detail.
body: Paul draws attention to his own handwriting: "ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand" (v.11). He usually dictated his letters to a scribe, but here he seems to have taken the pen himself — for this closing section, if not the whole letter — and wants the Galatians to notice.

Ancient writers sometimes added a personal note in their own hand to authenticate a dictated letter. Paul does that here and comments on it directly, a small but telling sign of how personally invested he is in a letter this urgent and confrontational.

chapters.title: Glorying Only in the Cross
chapters.teaser: Paul contrasts rivals who boast in Gentile conversions to their number with his own single boast.
body: Paul names a motive he suspects behind the whole controversy: "as many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ" (v.12). Pushing circumcision, in his reading, let rivals avoid persecution by making converts look conventionally Jewish.

He answers with his own single, non-negotiable boast: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world" (v.14). Not numbers of converts, not credentials — just the cross itself.

chapters.title: The Marks of Jesus
chapters.teaser: Paul offers his own scars as final proof of his authority, needing no further argument.
body: Paul closes the letter's argument with something no rival could counterfeit: "from henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus" (v.17) — physical scars from beatings and stoning endured for the gospel he's spent six chapters defending.

It's a fitting ending for the letter's whole method. Paul has argued theology, history, and Scripture at length, but his final word is his own body — proof that what he's asking the Galatians to hold onto has already cost him everything.
